Hepatotoxicity of Statins by HIV/HCV Status
Risk of Acute Liver Injury After Statin Initiation by Human

Background.  Patients with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) and/or chronic hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection may be 
prescribed statins as treatment for metabolic/cardiovascular disease, but it remains unclear if the risk of acute liver injury (ALI) is 
increased for statin initiators compared to nonusers in groups classified by HIV/HCV status.
Methods.  We conducted a cohort study to compare rates of ALI in statin initiators vs nonusers among 7686 HIV/HCV-
coinfected, 8155 HCV-monoinfected, 17 739 HIV-monoinfected, and 36 604 uninfected persons in the Veterans Aging Cohort Study 
(2000–2012). We determined development of (1) liver aminotransferases >200 U/L, (2) severe ALI (coagulopathy with hyperbiliru-
binemia), and (3) death, all within 18 months. Cox regression was used to determine propensity score–adjusted hazard ratios (HRs) 
with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) of outcomes in statin initiators compared to nonusers across the groups.
Results.  Among HIV/HCV-coinfected patients, statin initiators had lower risks of aminotransferase levels >200 U/L (HR, 0.66 
[95% CI, .53–.83]), severe ALI (HR, 0.23 [95% CI, .12–.46]), and death (HR, 0.36 [95% CI, .28–.46]) compared with statin nonusers. 
In the setting of chronic HCV alone, statin initiators had reduced risks of aminotransferase elevations (HR, 0.57 [95% CI, .45–.72]), 
severe ALI (HR, 0.15 [95% CI, .06–.37]), and death (HR, 0.42 [95% CI, .32–.54]) than nonusers. Among HIV-monoinfected patients, 
statin initiators had lower risks of aminotransferase increases (HR, 0.52 [95% CI, .40–.66]), severe ALI (HR, 0.26 [95% CI, .13–.55]), 
and death (HR, 0.19 [95% CI, .16–.23]) compared with nonusers. Results were similar among uninfected persons.
Conclusions.  Regardless of HIV and/or chronic HCV status, statin initiators had a lower risk of ALI and death within 18 months 
compared with statin nonusers.
Keywords.  statins; HIV; hepatitis C; hepatotoxicity; acute liver injury.
 
Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) and chronic hepati-
tis C virus (HCV) infection each contribute to metabolic and 
cardiovascular diseases [1–5]. The 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutar-
yl-coenzyme reductase inhibitors (statins) may be prescribed 
to HIV- and/or chronic HCV-infected patients as part of a 
treatment regimen for these conditions [6]. Implementation 
of new hyperlipidemia treatment guidelines is predicted to 
increase eligibility for statin therapy in the United States [7], 
including among those with HIV and chronic HCV [8]. Recent 
studies have particularly highlighted the beneficial effects of 
statins in chronic HCV, such as higher rates of sustained viro-
logic response to antiviral therapy [9, 10], decreased rates of 
hepatocellular carcinoma [11], and decreased risk of hepatic 
decompensation and death in the setting of cirrhosis [12–15]. 
However, statins may also be associated with acute liver injury 
(ALI) and have been implicated as causes of acute liver failure 
[16–19].
Despite the increasing use of statin therapy and potential con-
sequences of statin-induced ALI, it remains unclear if patients 
prescribed a statin are at increased risk of ALI compared to 
statin nonusers in the setting of HIV/HCV coinfection, HCV

monoinfection, and HIV monoinfection. HCV-associated liver 
disease could alter the pharmacokinetics and hepatic metabo-
lism of medications [20, 21], and might increase the risk and/
or severity of drug-induced ALI [21–23]. HIV-related immune 
dysregulation and oxidative stress, HIV-induced hepatocyte 
apoptosis, and antiretroviral therapy (ART) might also con-
tribute to the risk of statin-induced ALI [24]. As clinical trials 
of statins excluded patients with HIV and chronic HCV [16], 
analyses that evaluate the hepatotoxicity of statins among these 
patients in clinical practice settings are important to ensure 
their safety in these populations.
To address this knowledge gap, we evaluated the risk of ALI 
in statin initiators vs nonusers among HIV/HCV-coinfected, 
HCV-monoinfected, HIV-monoinfected, and uninfected per-
sons. Our goal was to determine if the risk of ALI was higher 
for statin initiators compared to individuals who were never 
prescribed statin therapy across these groups.
METHODS
Study Design and Data Source
We conducted a retrospective cohort study of HIV/HCV-
coinfected, HCV-monoinfected, HIV-monoinfected, and unin-
fected persons using data from the Veterans Aging Cohort 
Study (VACS) between 1 January 2000 and 30 September 2012 
[25]. The VACS consists of electronic medical record data from 
HIV-infected patients receiving care at Veterans Affairs (VA) 
medical facilities across the United States. At each site where 
an HIV-infected patient was identified, 2 uninfected patients 
matched on age, sex, and race/ethnicity were selected. Available 
data include demographic characteristics, hospital and outpa-
tient diagnoses (recorded using International Classification of 
Diseases, Ninth Revision [ICD-9] codes), procedures, laboratory 
results, and dispensed medications. Date of death is ascertained 
from the VA Vital Status file [26]. US Medicare claims data were 
available for Veterans also enrolled in this program and were 
merged with the VACS data. The study was approved by the 
institutional review boards of the University of Pennsylvania, 
VA Connecticut Healthcare System, and Yale University.
Study Patients
Eligible patients attended primary care/internal medicine, 
cardiology, endocrinology, gastroenterology, geriatrics, hepa-
tology, infectious diseases, or women’s health clinics in the 
VA system. These clinics were chosen because they were the 
source of 85% of statin use, and we wanted to ensure that sta-
tin initiators and nonusers came from the same source popu-
lation [12].
HIV infection was determined by a positive HIV antibody 
and/or RNA. Chronic HCV was determined by the presence of 
detectable HCV RNA. HIV/HCV-uninfected persons had no 
ICD-9 diagnosis or laboratory evidence of either HIV or HCV 
infection.
Among the HIV/HCV-coinfected, HCV-monoinfected, HIV-
monoinfected, and uninfected persons, statin initiators had at 
least 1 outpatient prescription for any statin (atorvastatin, flu-
vastatin, lovastatin, pravastatin, rosuvastatin, or simvastatin) 
dispensed within the VA for a period of >1 month, with the prior 
12  months being statin-free. For statin initiators, we defined 
the index date as the date that a statin was initially dispensed. 
Statin nonusers never had a fill for any drugs in this class, and 
a randomly selected outpatient visit date was used as the index 
date for start of follow-up for this group. To ensure that patients 
received medications from the VA (and minimize the likelihood 
that patients received a statin prescription from outside the VA), 
prior to their index date, all patients had to have at least 1 year of 
care in the VA system and receive a prescription fill for any drug.
Patients were excluded if they (1) had unknown HCV status, 
(2) had positive hepatitis B surface antigen (to isolate the effect 
of chronic HCV), (3) had evidence of any ALI outcome (defined 
below) prior to the index date, or (4) used warfarin during the 
study period (preventing identification of coagulopathy due to 
severe ALI).
The 12 months prior to the index date represented the baseline 
period, during which baseline comorbidities, laboratory results, 
and medications were collected. Follow-up continued until study 
endpoint, death, discontinuation of ART (no further statin fills 
within 30 days after the last prescription’s supply), 18 months 
after index date, or last VA contact before 30 September 2012. 
We evaluated outcomes over 18 months, as statin-induced ALI 
typically develops within 18 months of initiation [18, 19].
Main Study Outcomes
To determine the full spectrum of ALI events associated with 
statin initiation, we examined 4 categories of outcomes within 
18 months of the start of follow-up. First, we determined devel-
opment of severe liver aminotransferase elevations, defined as 
an inpatient or outpatient alanine aminotransferase (ALT) or 
aspartate aminotransferase (AST) >200 U/L (approximately 
5 times the upper limit of normal [ULN] of the assays used, 
a threshold that represents clinically important hepatic injury 
[27], and approximately 10 times what has been considered nor-
mal liver aminotransferase levels for males [30 U/L] and females 
[19 U/L] [28]). Second, we evaluated severe ALI, defined by 1 
inpatient or outpatient international normalized ratio (INR) 
≥1.5 and total bilirubin >2 times ULN within 30 days of each 
other. This definition indicates severe hepatic dysfunction 
and has been used by the US Food and Drug Administration’s 
Sentinel Initiative to assess serious drug-induced hepatotox-
icity in the postmarketing period [29]. Third, we determined 
hospitalizations with an ICD-9 diagnosis suggestive of ALI 
(Supplementary Table  1) recorded within the VA system or 
Medicare (to capture events occurring at non-VA hospitals that 
did not result in transfer to a VA facility). Finally, we examined 
all-cause mortality.

Hepatotoxicity of Statins by HIV/HCV Status
Data Collection
Baseline demographic and clinical data included age, sex, race/
ethnicity, body mass index, year of statin initiation, relevant 
medical comorbidities, antiviral treatment for chronic HCV, 
exposure to potentially hepatotoxic antiretrovirals (abaca-
vir, didanosine, nevirapine, saquinavir, stavudine, tipranavir, 
or zalcitabine [30]), and exposure to potentially hepatotoxic 
nonantiretroviral drugs (defined below). Medical comorbidi-
ties included alcohol dependence/abuse, cerebrovascular dis-
ease, chronic kidney disease, cirrhosis, congestive heart failure, 
diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidemia, hypertension, injection/ 
noninjection drug use, peripheral vascular disease, and myo-
cardial infarction and were determined based on occurrence 
of at least 1 hospital ICD-9 diagnosis or 2 outpatient diagnoses 
(to reduce likelihood of misclassification). Use of potentially 
hepatotoxic nonantiretroviral medications was determined by 
a prescription fill for acetaminophen (alone or in combination 
with an opioid), duloxetine, isoniazid, metformin, thiazolidin-
ediones, or valproic acid. These drugs were selected because of 
their known potential for ALI [31] and frequent use by HIV 
and/or chronic HCV-infected patients in the VACS [32, 33].
Baseline laboratory data on ALT, AST, albumin, total biliru-
bin, INR, total cholesterol, high-density lipoprotein, low-density 
lipoprotein, triglycerides, hemoglobin, and platelet count were 
collected from dates closest to, but within 12 months prior to, 
the index date. The Fibrosis-4 Index for Liver Fibrosis (FIB-4), 
a noninvasive measure of hepatic fibrosis, was calculated using 
baseline AST, ALT, platelet count, and age as follows: (age [years] 
× AST [U/L]) / ((platelet count [109/L]) × (ALT [U/L])1/2) [34]. 
FIB-4 scores <1.45 identify no/minimal hepatic fibrosis, and 
scores >3.25 indicate advanced fibrosis/cirrhosis.
Data collected during follow-up included outpatient and 
inpatient ALT, AST, INR, and total bilirubin results and dates 
of measurement; principal hospital discharge ICD-9 diagnoses 
suggestive of ALI (Supplementary Table 1) recorded within the 
VA or Medicare data and dates recorded; and date of death.
Statistical Analysis
We first estimated incidence rates of outcomes (in events/1000 
person-years) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for statin 
initiators and nonusers in the HIV/HCV-coinfected, HCV-
monoinfected, HIV-monoinfected, and uninfected groups.
Because of the many potential confounding variables relative 
to the number of ALI events, we used propensity scores to con-
trol for confounding by indication [35]. The propensity score 
model was developed using logistic regression, with potential 
determinants of statin therapy as independent variables and 
statin exposure as the dependent variable. The propensity score 
model included all variables in Table 1 (except mean follow-up) 
and several interactions.
Cox regression was used to estimate hazard ratios (HRs) of 
outcomes in statin initiators vs nonusers in each of the 4 groups,

adjusting for propensity score [36]. We adjusted for, rather than 
stratified or matched on, propensity score within multivari-
able models because (1) there were too few outcomes within 
some propensity score strata to perform stratification, and (2) 
unmatched statin initiators would have been excluded, reducing 
power to detect associations. We confirmed the adequacy of the 
propensity score as a continuous variable by (1) observing over-
lap in their distribution between statin initiators and nonusers, 
and (2) demonstrating linearity of propensity score categories 
within outcome models. Covariates in the Cox model included 
propensity score, statin use (initiation vs not), HIV (present vs 
absent), HCV (present vs absent), and the interaction between 
statin initiation, HIV, and HCV (statin*HIV*HCV). HRs were 
determined from the statin*HIV*HCV interaction. To assess 
whether baseline hepatic fibrosis stage affected the risk of ALI 
and death associated with statin initiation across the groups, we 
evaluated HRs of outcomes after stratifying on baseline FIB-4 
score (<1.45; 1.45–3.25; >3.25).
Proportionality of hazards was assessed by log-log plots and 
Schoenfeld residuals [36]. Propensity score models were devel-
oped using SAS version 9.4 software (SAS Institute, Cary, North 
Carolina), and outcomes were analyzed using Stata version 14.1 
software (StataCorp, College Station, Texas).
RESULTS
Patient Characteristics
Among 143 100 patients enrolled in the VACS through 
September 2012, we identified 55 366 statin initiators and 
75 085 statin nonusers. After exclusions, 27 303 statin initiators 
(1437 HIV/HCV; 2331 HCV; 5902 HIV; 17 633 uninfected) 
and 42 881 statin nonusers (6249 HIV/HCV; 5824 HCV; 11 837 
HIV; 18 971 uninfected) remained (Figure 1).
Across the 4 groups, statin initiators were older; had a higher 
prevalence of obesity; more commonly were prescribed a 
potentially hepatotoxic medication; and more frequently had 
cerebrovascular disease, chronic kidney disease, heart failure, 
diabetes, hyperlipidemia, hypertension, myocardial infarction, 
and peripheral vascular disease compared with statin nonus-
ers (Table 1). HCV treatment was uncommon in patients with 
HIV/HCV or HCV alone (Table 1).
Unadjusted Incidence Rates of Acute Liver Injury Events and Death
Table  2 reports the unadjusted incidence rates of liver ami-
notransferases >200 U/L, severe ALI, hospitalization with an 
ALI diagnosis, and death, all within 18 months, for each of the 
groups. Regardless of HIV or chronic HCV status, statin initia-
tors had lower rates of each ALI outcome and death compared 
with statin nonusers.
Risk of Acute Liver Injury and Death in Statin Initiators Versus Nonusers, 
By Human Immunodeficiency Virus/Hepatitis C Virus Status
After propensity score adjustment, the risks of liver ami-
notransferases >200 U/L, severe ALI, hospitalization with an 
ALI diagnosis, and death were significantly lower in statin ini-
tiators than nonusers among the HIV/HCV-coinfected, HCV-
monoinfected, HIV-monoinfected, and uninfected groups 
(Table  3). Point estimates of the HRs of each endpoint were 
similar in magnitude across the group comparisons. Similar 
findings were observed when analyses were stratified by base-
line FIB-4 score (Supplementary Table 2). Even in the setting 
of advanced hepatic fibrosis/cirrhosis (FIB-4 >3.25), statin ini-
tiators had a lower risk of ALI and death compared with statin 
nonusers across the groups classified by HIV/HCV status.
DISCUSSION
The hepatic safety of statins in the setting of HIV and/or 
chronic HCV has remained unclear and has been a concern for 
clinicians. In this study, we found that statin initiators had lower

incidence rates and risk of all ALI endpoints and death within 
18 months compared to statin nonusers, regardless of HIV or 
chronic HCV status. Across the groups evaluated, the HRs of 
each outcome were similar in magnitude, suggesting that nei-
ther HIV or chronic HCV modified associations between sta-
tin initiation and ALI events. Similar findings were observed 
when analyses were stratified by baseline FIB-4. Taken together, 
these data demonstrate the hepatic safety of statins in patients 
with HIV/HCV coinfection, HCV monoinfection, and HIV 
monoinfection, even in the setting of advanced hepatic fibrosis/
cirrhosis. Clinicians should therefore not be reluctant to pre-
scribe statins to patients with these chronic infections.
Our findings are consistent with 2 prior small observational 
studies examining hepatotoxicity after statin initiation among 
HCV-infected persons. One retrospective analysis from the 
VA Palo Alto Healthcare System found that the incidence of 
mild to moderate liver aminotransferase increases (AST or 
ALT up to 10 times ULN), severe ALI (total bilirubin >3.0 mg/
dL), and discontinuation of statin therapy as a result of hepa-
totoxicity was similar between 166 anti-HCV-positive and 332 
anti-HCV-negative statin initiators [37]. A second retrospective 
study from the Michael E. DeBakey VA Medical Center exam-
ined changes in aminotransferases in 20 HCV-infected statin 
users who were matched on age, stage of hepatic fibrosis, and 
time since HCV diagnosis to 64 HCV-infected statin nonusers 
[38]. In the setting of chronic HCV, statin initiators had larger 
declines in aminotransferases from baseline through 1 year of 
follow-up compared to nonusers. To our knowledge, no prior 
studies have evaluated the risk of ALI associated with statin 
initiation among HIV/HCV-coinfected or HIV-monoinfected 
persons.
The lower risk of ALI in statin initiators vs nonusers, regard-
less of HIV or chronic HCV status and stage of hepatic fibro-
sis by FIB-4, might be due, in part, to the anti-inflammatory 
effects of statins in hepatocytes and vascular endothelial cells 
[39, 40]. Statins might also slow HCV-associated liver fibrosis 
progression [41, 42] and promote intrahepatic vasodilation and 
reduce portal pressure, which might improve liver function and 
decrease complications of portal hypertension [43].
Our study should be interpreted within the context of sev-
eral potential limitations. First, we undertook these analyses 
from an epidemiological standpoint, comparing the relative 
incidences and rates of ALI events and death among the groups 
to identify hepatotoxicity signals; however, we were unable to 
ascertain the etiology of each ALI event given the large num-
bers of each outcome across the groups. Second, misclassifica-
tion of drug exposure is possible as statin adherence cannot be 
confirmed. However, we expect misclassification to be mini-
mal as this was determined from pharmacy dispensing records. 
Third, there is the potential that this analysis could have been 
subject to ascertainment bias, as patients who were initiated on 
a statin might have had liver-related laboratory tests assessed

more frequently than those who did not use a statin. However, 
we also evaluated clinical ALI endpoints that were not reliant 
on liver-related laboratory testing, specifically hospitalization 
with an ALI diagnosis and all-cause mortality, which should 
not have been subject to differential ascertainment. Results 
of analyses of these endpoints were similar to those of liver 
aminotransferases >200 U/L and severe ALI. Fourth, there is 
potential for confounding by indication [44], as patients were 
assigned to statin treatment by clinician choice. Our use of 
propensity scores attempted to account for this. There is also 
the potential for confounding by hepatotoxic medication use. 
However, across all 4 groups, statin initiators were more likely 
to receive a potentially hepatotoxic medication than nonusers. 
Thus, the results of our analyses demonstrating lower risks of 
ALI and death in statin initiators compared to nonusers across 
all groups are likely conservative. Fifth, because of limited use 
of some statins within the VA system, we did not evaluate the 
comparative risk of ALI associated with individual statins by 
HCV status. We also did not collect data on statin dose, so were 
unable to determine if there was a dose-response relationship 
with ALI events and death. Finally, our study sample was pre-
dominantly comprised of male US Veterans, and results may 
not be generalizable to women.
Our study had a number of strengths. We included large sam-
ple sizes of patients grouped by HIV and chronic HCV status, 
and used propensity scores to adjust for many important con-
founding variables. Importantly, we observed consistent find-
ings across the spectrum of ALI endpoints evaluated.
In conclusion, we found that statin initiators had lower inci-
dence rates and risk of ALI and death within 18 months com-
pared with statin nonusers, regardless of HIV or chronic HCV 
status. Even in the setting of advanced hepatic fibrosis/cirrho-
sis, statin initiation was associated with a lower risk of ALI and 
death across the groups. These findings demonstrate the hepatic 
safety of statins in patients with HIV/HCV coinfection, HCV 
monoinfection, and HIV monoinfection.
